subject: physics
title: Conservation laws and particle equations
key_idea: In every particle interaction, charge, baryon number and lepton number are conserved, along with energy and momentum. Add each quantity before and after to test whether an equation is possible. In β decay, one quark changes flavour through the weak interaction.

blocks.text: An interaction can only happen if certain quantities are the same before and after. Each one is found by adding the values for every particle.

items: **Charge**, **baryon number** and **lepton number** are conserved in every interaction.
Nucleon number and charge are conserved in nuclear processes.
**Energy** and **momentum** are conserved. Mass can become energy and energy can become mass.
Quarks have baryon number +⅓ and antiquarks −⅓, so a baryon has baryon number +1.
Charge, baryon number and lepton number must be equal before and after.
Energy and momentum are always conserved.

blocks.text: To decide whether an interaction is possible, add each quantity on both sides of the equation.

items.text: Write down the charge, baryon number and lepton number of every particle.
Add each quantity on the left, then on the right.
If any quantity differs, the interaction cannot happen.

items: Neutron decay, n → p + e⁻ + ν̄: charge 0 = +1 − 1 + 0, baryon number 1 = 1, lepton number 0 = 0 + 1 − 1. It is allowed.
If the antineutrino is left out, the lepton number changes from 0 to +1, so the equation is not allowed.
An antineutrino (not a neutrino) is emitted in β⁻ decay, to balance the electron's lepton number.

sections.heading: Beta decay as a change of quark

blocks.text: Beta decay happens through the weak interaction. It changes one quark into another quark of a different flavour inside a nucleon.

items: β⁻ decay: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄. Charge: −⅓ → +⅔ − 1 = −⅓ (balanced).
β⁺ decay: u → d + e⁺ + ν. Charge: +⅔ → −⅓ + 1 = +⅔ (balanced).
The neutron is udd and becomes uud, which is a proton.
The proton is uud and becomes udd, which is a neutron.
β⁺ decay happens inside a proton-rich nucleus. A free proton does not decay this way.
β⁻ decay of a nucleus: the proton number goes up by 1 and the nucleon number stays the same.
β⁺ decay of a nucleus: the proton number goes down by 1 and the nucleon number stays the same.
β⁻ decay: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄. β⁺ decay: u → d + e⁺ + ν.
Balance charge on each side of a quark equation.

checks.q: Explain why the neutron decay n → p + e⁻ is not allowed, and write the equation that is.
checks.a: Lepton number is 0 before and +1 after, so it is not conserved. The correct equation is n → p + e⁻ + ν̄, in which the antineutrino has lepton number −1.

checks.q: Write the quark equation for β⁺ decay and show that charge is conserved.
checks.a: u → d + e⁺ + ν. Charge before = +⅔; after = −⅓ + 1 + 0 = +⅔.

checks.q: State the change in quark composition when a neutron undergoes β⁻ decay.
checks.a: A down quark changes into an up quark, so udd becomes uud (a proton).

items: **Strangeness** is also conserved in strong interactions. In weak interactions it can change by 0, +1 or −1.
Strange particles are always produced in pairs, so that total strangeness stays zero.
Example: K⁺ → π⁺ + π⁰ has strangeness +1 → 0. The change of 1 is allowed because it is a weak decay.
Data for particles outside those on the course is given in the question.
Energy and momentum are conserved in all interactions.

blocks.text: Use conservation of charge, energy and momentum to interpret particle tracks in a magnetic field.

items: Oppositely charged particles curve in opposite directions.
A neutral particle leaves no track.
A track with a smaller radius has less momentum, because r = p / BQ.
A pair created from a photon appears as two tracks curving apart from one point, with equal and opposite charges.
A track that spirals inwards is a particle losing energy.
If the tracks of the decay products do not balance the momentum, a neutral particle that left no track carried it away.
Nucleon number and charge are conserved in nuclear processes.
Alpha decay: the nucleon number falls by 4 and the proton number by 2.
An electron antineutrino is produced in β⁻ decay and an electron neutrino in β⁺ decay.
β⁻ decay is written d → u + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄ and β⁺ decay is u → d + ⁰₊₁e + ν.
Check the charge on each side of a quark equation, using +⅔ for u and −⅓ for d.
Other hadron decays can also be written as quark changes. Add the quark charges to check them.
